question.text: Among the five option Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, Rho), which is generally considered the LEAST significant for short-term option trading?

answer.text: Rho, because interest rates change slowly and their impact on short-dated options is minimal
Delta, because underlying price changes are unpredictable
Theta, because time decay is negligible for short-term options
Gamma, because delta remains relatively stable for most options

explanation.text: The Logic: Rho measures sensitivity of option price to changes in the risk-free interest rate. For short-term options, two factors make this small in practice: interest rates change slowly relative to underlying prices and volatility, and the present-value effect of rate moves on a short-dated contract is modest. Delta, gamma, theta and vega usually dominate the day-to-day P&L of a short-dated options book, while rho matters far more for long-dated instruments such as LEAPS. The Trap: Delta drives directional P&L and is far from negligible. Gamma matters most for short-dated ATM options and cannot be ignored. Theta is in fact most significant — not least — for short-term options, since time decay accelerates near expiry. Note: The cited NISM-Series-VIII workbook pages (77-78, 123-124) list and define the Greeks but do not state that "Rho is generally the least significant Greek for short-term option trading". The framing above is general options-Greeks practice rather than a direct workbook citation.
